notes.t: Cloud's v5e page (2026-10-13) gives HBM bandwidth as "800 GiBps", which read literally is 859 GB/s; the scaling book and jax/_src/tpu_info.py give 8.2e11 B/s (819 GB/s). This page keeps 819 GB/s, as the Reading tab and the Hardware topic do; with 859 GB/s the ridge point would be 229 instead of 241.

v5p HBM bandwidth: Cloud docs 2,765 GBps; jax/_src/tpu_info.py 2.46e12 B/s (it splits 2.46e12 across the 2 TensorCores); the scaling book 2.8e12. The roofline here uses Cloud's figure; with tpu_info's the ridge point would be 187 instead of 166.
v5p HBM: Cloud 95 GiB (102 GB); tpu_info 103,000,000,000 bytes; scaling book 96GB. Same memory, different rounding and units.

Peak = TensorCores x MXUs x side^2 x 2 FLOPs x clock reproduces v4 (275 TF at 1,050 MHz) and v5e (197 TF at 1.5 GHz). For v6e (1 TensorCore x 2 MXUs of 256 x 256, Cloud and tpu_info agree) it needs a 3.5 GHz clock, and for 7x (2 x 2 x 256 x 256, tpu_info) 4.4 GHz, far above any published TPU clock. Either the per-MXU rate is not side^2 MACs per cycle on these chips or a count is wrong; Google publishes neither clock. Unconfirmed; the Hardware topic's TPU page shows the same gap for v6e.

TPU7x has 2 TensorCores per chip (one per chiplet) and no megacore (tpu_info.py: supports_megacore is True only for v4 and v5p), so each TensorCore is a separate JAX device: a 4-chip host shows 8 devices. On v4 and v5p the two cores are fused into one device by default.

Per-chip ICI: Cloud gives 400 (v5e), 800 (v6e), 1,200 (v5p, 7x) GBps bidirectional. The scaling book's per-link figures times the link count give 360, 720, 1,080 and 1,080 GB/s: the same order, about 10% lower each time. Use per-link numbers for a single ring, per-chip numbers only when every link is busy.

free.t: TPU Research Cloud: accepted researchers get Cloud TPUs "at no charge" from "a cluster of more than 1,000 Cloud TPU devices"; in return they share their research (papers, open code, blog posts) and give Google feedback. Quota is granted "on a temporary basis"; other Google Cloud services (the VM, storage) are not free. Neither page names TPU generations or a duration.

Colab's FAQ: "The types of GPUs and TPUs that are available in Colab vary over time"; "Colab does not publish these limits"; free notebooks "can run for at most 12 hours"; "Colab resources are not guaranteed and not unlimited". So the TPU type and quota on Colab are not published; check the runtime menu on the day.

Kaggle's TPU documentation page renders only in a browser and could not be read. Third-party guides say 20 hours a week and 9-hour sessions; they disagree on the chip (TPU v3-8 in older guides, TPU v5e-8 in a 2025 article). Kaggle shows your remaining quota in account settings. The old page's "20 h/month" matches no source.

sources.vmem_quote: VMEM ... much smaller than HBM (for example, 128 MiB on TPU v5e) ... VMEM bandwidth is around 22x higher than HBM bandwidth which means an MXU operation reading from/writing to VMEM requires an arithmetic intensity of only 10-20
